## Purpose

This procedure describes the operation and maintenance of the
ultrasonic bath and probe sonicator used in the EA Program laboratory.
Sonication uses high-frequency sound waves (typically 20--40 kHz) to
generate cavitation bubbles in a liquid medium. The collapse of these
bubbles produces localized shear forces that disaggregate particles,
disperse samples, degas solutions, enhance extraction, and clean
labware. In the EA Program, sonication is used for soil particle
dispersion, glassware cleaning, sample homogenization, and cell lysis
in DNA extraction workflows.


## Scope

- **Applies to:** The Fisher Scientific ultrasonic bath (SGM 134) and
  any probe-tip sonicators available in EA Program laboratories
- **Does not apply to:** Vortex mixing (see future SOP-L104); bead
  beating for DNA extraction (integral to the extraction protocol in
  [SOP-L700](SOP-L700-dna-extraction.qmd)); industrial-scale
  ultrasonics
- **Location:** SGM 134

## Definitions

- **Amplitude:** The peak displacement of the sonicator probe tip,
  expressed as a percentage of maximum; higher amplitude delivers more
  energy per unit time to the sample.
- **Cavitation:** The formation and violent collapse of microscopic
  bubbles in liquid exposed to ultrasound; the primary mechanism by
  which ultrasound disrupts cells and disperses particles.
- **Duty cycle:** For pulsed sonication, the fraction of each cycle
  during which the probe is active (e.g., 0.5 s on / 0.5 s off = 50%
  duty cycle); used to limit heat input to sensitive samples.
- **Probe sonicator (ultrasonic processor):** A device that converts
  electrical energy to ultrasonic vibrations (typically 20 kHz) via a
  piezoelectric transducer; the probe tip vibrates in direct contact
  with the sample.
- **Sonication bath:** An ultrasonic cleaning bath in which the sample
  container is immersed in water through which ultrasound is
  transmitted; less intense than probe sonication; used for dispersing
  particles or aiding extraction.
- **Specific energy (J mL^-1^):** Total ultrasonic energy delivered
  per unit volume; the parameter most predictive of cell disruption
  yield for a given sample type; increases with amplitude, time, and
  volume.

## Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Hearing:** Ultrasonic baths produce audible noise (buzzing/
  humming) during operation. Probe sonicators at high power can
  produce high-intensity noise. Wear hearing protection if exposure
  exceeds a few minutes at high power settings.
- **Aerosol generation:** Probe sonication of open samples generates
  aerosols. If the sample contains hazardous biological or chemical
  material, sonicate inside a fume hood or biological safety cabinet.
- **Heat:** Extended sonication heats the bath water and the sample.
  Monitor temperature if heat-sensitive analytes are involved.
- **Skin contact:** Do not immerse hands in the bath while it is
  operating. Cavitation can damage skin tissue.
- **Glassware:** Thin-walled or cracked glassware may fail under
  sonication. Use containers rated for ultrasonic use.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Safety glasses
- [ ] Nitrile gloves
- [ ] Lab coat
- [ ] Hearing protection (for probe sonication at high power or
      extended bath sonication)

### Emergency Procedures

For chemical spills from broken containers, follow
[SOP-L004 Chemical Spill Response](SOP-L004-chemical-spill-response.qmd).
If the sonicator sparks, smokes, or produces unusual odors, unplug
immediately and report to the lab manager.

## Procedure

### Ultrasonic Bath

#### Setup

1. Fill the bath with deionized water to the manufacturer's
   recommended level (typically 2--3 cm above the transducer surface
   or to the fill line). Do not operate the bath without water; this
   damages the transducer.
2. If using the bath for cleaning, add the appropriate detergent
   concentration per [SOP-L101](SOP-L101-glassware-cleaning.qmd)
3. Degas the bath water by running the sonicator for 5 minutes
   without a load (degassed water transmits ultrasonic energy more
   effectively)

#### Operation

1. Place sample containers (tubes, beakers, flasks) in the bath using
   a rack or holder. Containers should be partially submerged but not
   resting on the bath floor (direct contact with the floor can cause
   hot spots and uneven sonication).
2. Set the timer for the duration specified in the analytical SOP
   (typical ranges: 1--15 minutes for sample dispersion, 15--30
   minutes for glassware cleaning)
3. If the bath has a heater, set the temperature as required (common:
   room temperature for samples, 40--50 C for cleaning)
4. Start the sonicator. Verify cavitation by observing fine bubbles
   rising from the bath surface.
5. Do not open the lid or reach into the bath during operation
6. When the timer stops, remove containers using tongs or gloves

#### Post-Use

1. Turn off the sonicator
2. If the bath water is visibly contaminated, drain, rinse, and refill
   with fresh DI water
3. Replace the bath water at least weekly even if it appears clean
4. Wipe the exterior with a damp cloth

### Probe Sonicator

#### Setup

1. Select the appropriate tip (microtip for volumes less than 10 mL;
   standard tip for 10--50 mL)
2. Attach the tip securely; a loose tip reduces energy transfer and
   can damage the probe
3. Clamp the probe in a ring stand so the tip is immersed in the
   sample to approximately one-third of the liquid depth. Do not
   touch the container walls or bottom with the tip.

#### Operation

1. Set the power level and pulse settings per the analytical SOP
   (common: 20--40% amplitude, 5 seconds on / 5 seconds off pulsing
   to minimize heating)
2. If the sample is hazardous, work inside a fume hood or biological
   safety cabinet with the sash lowered
3. Start sonication. A faint hissing and visible agitation confirm
   cavitation.
4. Monitor sample temperature; if overheating is a concern, place the
   sample container in an ice bath during sonication
5. After the prescribed duration, stop the sonicator

#### Post-Use

1. Immediately wipe the probe tip with a lint-free tissue dampened
   with 70% ethanol or DI water
2. For molecular biology work (eDNA, PCR), decontaminate the tip with
   10% bleach, rinse with DI water, then wipe with 70% ethanol
3. Inspect the tip for pitting or erosion; a heavily pitted tip
   reduces performance and should be replaced


## Maintenance

| Task                                  | Frequency              |
|:--------------------------------------|:-----------------------|
| Replace bath water                    | Weekly                 |
| Clean bath interior (drain, wipe, refill) | Weekly             |
| Inspect probe tip for pitting         | Before each use        |
| Replace probe tip                     | When pitted or eroded  |
| Check bath transducer (listen for changes in tone) | Monthly |


## Quality Control

- For soil particle dispersion, verify that the sonication time and
  power are sufficient by checking particle size distribution results
  against the analytical SOP's acceptance criteria
- For glassware cleaning, verify cleanliness by rinsing with DI water
  and checking for water sheeting (clean glass sheets evenly; dirty
  glass beads)
- If the bath fails to produce visible cavitation, contact the lab
  manager (the transducer may be failing)


## Waste Disposal

| Waste Type                    | Disposal Method                          |
|:------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Used bath water (no hazardous chemicals) | Drain                     |
| Used bath water (with detergent or chemicals) | Dispose per [SOP-L006](SOP-L006-waste-disposal.qmd) |
| Spent probe tips              | Standard trash (stainless steel)         |

## Training Record

Before operating the sonicator independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Demonstrate proper bath fill level and degassing
3. For probe sonicator users: demonstrate tip attachment, immersion
   depth, and power/pulse settings under supervision
4. Perform one sonication task under supervision
5. Be signed off by the PI or lab manager
